5.text: who approached the northern shore from the Kolyma side, the tents of the

6.text: Reindeer people appeared to be typical Chukchee dwellings. The difference,

7.text: was the more striking, since around Kuluˊči Bay the inhabitants turned from

8.text: maritime pursuits to reindeer-breeding. I know of some, whom I saw on the

9.text: northern tundra, who claim that their grandfathers lived on the coast and

10.text: occupied themselves with seal-hunting. This same change occurred in several

11.text: other places, as will be shown farther on.

12.text: It is not my intention to deny that on the Arctic coast there was previously

13.text: more of the Eskimo element, which little by little became assimilated by the

14.text: Chukchee. Thus, some of the Chukchee village names, both on the Arctic

15.text: and on the Pacific shores, have an Eskimo sound, and moreover, especially

16.text: in their Aiˊwan form, can be explained on the basis of the Eskimo language.

40.text: In regard to the legend cited by Wrangell, about the Eskimo chief Krächoj,

41.text: who is said to have emigrated across the sea to certain islands, I may say

42.text: that I too heard it among the Chukchee; but it is mythical in character, and

43.text: is connected with other tales about vanished tribes, similar to corresponding

44.text: tales of the Eskimo. It is true, however, that the northern Chukchee believe

45.text: that in some northern land, not very far distant from the continent of Asia,

46.text: there lives a race of men sprung from these ancient emigrants. This land is,

47.text: said to have been seen by the crew of a boat which drifted out into the open

48.text: sea. It corresponds to Wrangell’s Land, and I have heard from people from
